newsitem.title: USA: N.C. jury to decide soldier's fate in race murders.
newsitem.headline: N.C. jury to decide soldier's fate in race murders.

text.p: A North Carolina judge Tuesday put the fate of a white former paratrooper in the hands of a jury for the racially motivated killings of two black people.
Jurors were to begin deliberating Wednesday morning whether to give James Burmeister the death penalty or life in prison.

Burmeister, convicted Thursday on two counts of first degree murder, listened impassively as Superior Court Judge Coy Brewer spent more than 90 minutes instructing the seven-man, five-woman jury following closing arguments Tuesday.
Burmeister shot to death Michael James, 36, and Jackie Burden, 27, on Dec. 7, 1995, as they walked along an unpaved road in their neighbourhood.

Defence lawyer Carl Ivarsson told jurors that sentencing Burmeister to death would not bring back James and Burden, but a life sentence would transform the former U.S. Army soldier from a hunter into one of the hunted.
"We cannot turn back the hands of time. We cannot undo the tragedy," he said. "If you want to make Jim Burmeister the bait for the rest of his life, you can do it."

Prosecutor John Dickson, who told jurors during the trial that Burmeister represented "pure, unmitigated evil," said in closing arguments that no evidence was presented to indicate Burmeister's hatred for blacks, Jews and other minorities had changed.

"Who is to say this defendant still won't be a hunter in prison," he said. "The only way to assume that he will not hunt and kill again is to sentence him to death. We seek only justice. Let God have mercy on his soul."
Prosecutors also argued that Burmeister deserved the death penalty for the brutal and calculating manner in which he killed Burden and James.
Defence lawyers said the sudden death of Burmeister's sister led to his heavy drinking, stunting his emotional growth to the point that he was swayed by racist skinhead rhetoric that led him to kill.
The jury's only choices were the death penalty or life in prison with no parole for 25 years, and the decision will be binding. A death sentence would be automatically appealed.
